title: A header for the run log
prompt: Every nightly run starts its log with one row about where it ran and what it read. Write `solve(orders)` so it returns that row, built with `spark.createDataFrame`.
rules: Five columns, in this order: `spark_version` (text), `cores` (int), `shuffle_partitions` (int), `order_rows` (bigint) and `order_columns` (int).
`spark_version` is the session's Spark version, `cores` is how many tasks Spark can run at once here, and `shuffle_partitions` is the `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` setting as a number.
`order_rows` counts every row of `orders`, duplicates included, and `order_columns` counts its columns.
hints: The session knows its version, and `spark.sparkContext` knows how many cores it has. Both were in the lesson on the SparkSession.
`spark.conf.get(...)` always gives back text. An `INT` column won't take the text `"4"`, so turn it into a number with `int(...)`.
Put the five values in one tuple and give a schema string, so `cores` and the column count come out as `int` and the row count as `bigint`.
explanation: Gather five Python values, then build one row: `spark.version`, `spark.sparkContext.defaultParallelism`, `int(spark.conf.get("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions"))`, `orders.count()` and `len(orders.columns)`, with the schema `"spark_version STRING, cores INT, shuffle_partitions INT, order_rows BIGINT, order_columns INT"`. A setting always comes back as text, so without `int(...)` the `INT` column refuses `"4"`. `spark.default.parallelism` isn't set here, so reading it fails; `defaultParallelism` on the context gives the cores. Without a schema, every whole number would be guessed as `bigint`.
